tagline.text: Cebu's secret garden of lakes, caves, and white sand hidden away

location.label: Location
location.text: Camotes Islands, Cebu (San Francisco, Poro, Tudela, Pilar)

children.text: Four islands floating in the Camotes Sea between mainland Cebu and Leyte, where the guitar-shaped Lake Danao, clear cave pools, and the white sand of Santiago Bay all come together. Large resorts are scarce, making it a good place to experience unassuming island life.

The Camotes Islands are a cluster of islands in the Camotes Sea between mainland Cebu and Leyte to its east. They consist of Pacijan, Poro, Ponson, and the small island of Tulang; travelers mainly visit Pacijan Island (San Francisco) and Poro Island (Poro and Tudela), which are connected to each other by a causeway. Ponson Island forms its own municipality, Pilar, and being farther away, sees fewer visitors.
The islands have long carried the nickname "Lost Horizon of the South." Just
2 hours

by boat from Cebu City, yet with almost no large-scale development, they retain quiet roads winding through coconut groves, unassuming fishing villages, limestone caves, and clear lakes. A common story traces the islands' name to "camote," the Spanish word for sweet potato.

In the middle of Pacijan Island is Lake Danao, which looks like a guitar from above, and along the coasts of the two islands are scattered the wide white sand of Santiago Bay and resorts such as Mangodlong Rock (Pacijan Island) and Buho Rock (Poro Island), where you jump into the sea from cliffs. The limestone terrain across the islands holds several cave pools filled with groundwater, and slipping into the cool water to escape the midday heat is a big part of the fun of a Camotes trip.

This is a place better suited to those who prefer renting a motorbike and unhurriedly touring beaches and caves one by one than to anyone seeking flashy nightlife or big resorts — free spirits and families of Korean expats looking for a weekend escape close to Cebu.

A roughly 680-hectare freshwater lake in San Francisco on Pacijan Island; you can rent a raft or kayak at the lakeside park and drift over the calm water. Zipline facilities also sometimes operate around the lake.
A broad, curving stretch of white sand on the south side of Pacijan Island, considered the most photogenic beach in Camotes. The water is clear and the waves gentle, making it good for family swims.
Timubo Cave in San Francisco has a staircase leading down to a clear underground pool beneath stalactites. The entrance fee is low, and the cool water makes it a good midday stop.
Bukilat Cave in Tudela, Poro Island, is a large cave where sunlight pours in through an opening in the ceiling, making for striking beams-of-light photos.
At cliffside resorts such as Mangodlong Rock and Buho Rock, you can jump from a few meters up into the clear sea. Non-guests can also enter for an admission or usage fee.

blocks.title: Mangrove causeway and touring the islands

children.text: A motorbike loop around both islands, passing mangrove forests near the causeway that links Pacijan and Poro, takes only half a day. Hills on the Poro Island side offer views of the sea toward Leyte.
Tulang Diyot Island, reached by small boat from the village of Tulang Daku at the northern tip of San Francisco, is a small island with white sand and clear water.

The dry season,
December–May
, is best overall, and within it,
March–May
— with calm seas and clear skies — is ideal for beaches and cliff diving. During
December–February

June–November
is the rainy season, with frequent afternoon showers, and cave pools can turn cloudy after heavy rain. From
August to November

During Holy Week, the
May

Most accommodations cluster around Santiago Bay on Pacijan Island and the coast of San Francisco. Mid-range beachfront resorts run about
a night, and village guesthouses are around

. Poro Island has a few clifftop resorts, good for a quiet sea view, but with fewer restaurants and amenities. High-end resorts are rare across the islands and facilities tend to be modest, so set your expectations accordingly.
Food centers on unassuming local dishes. Carinderias (local eateries) around the port and market serve grilled fish caught that day, kinilaw (fish cured in vinegar), and adobo for about

. Resort restaurants also serve seafood dishes alongside simple Western food, and many places do a beach barbecue in the evening. As the islands' name suggests, sweet potato and cassava snacks are common too, so try some at the market.
The islands have only a handful of ATMs that frequently run out of cash. It's best to withdraw all the cash you'll need in Cebu or Danao.
Some stretches have few gas stations for motorbike rentals, so use the bottled gasoline sold at village shops and keep your tank well topped up.
Most island roads are paved, but access roads to caves and beaches can be unpaved or steep. If you're a beginner rider, it's safer to go with a habal-habal driver.
Cave pools have slippery floors and cold water, so bring aqua shoes and a light waterproof bag.
Ferries often don't have assigned seating, so the earlier you board, the better your seat. The first morning boat can sell out early.
Phone signal generally reaches villages and beaches but drops out inside caves and on remote coastlines.
Good photo spots are the curving shoreline of Santiago Bay, the light beams in Bukilat Cave, and the morning mist over Lake Danao.
Always confirm the depth and tide conditions with on-site staff before cliff diving. Rocks are exposed and very dangerous at low tide.
Cave interiors have weak lighting and steep stairs. Children and elderly visitors should hold the railing and move slowly.
Avoid traveling by small boat in bad sea weather. The ro-ro ferry can also be cancelled, so check notices.
There are almost no streetlights at night, making motorbike riding dangerous. Avoid long-distance riding after dark.
Using soap or shampoo, and littering, are banned at natural attractions such as the lake and caves.
During Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) in
November 2025

, Typhoon Signal No. 4 was raised over the Camotes Islands and northeastern Cebu, including Danao, suffered heavy damage. Some resorts and attractions may still be under repair or may have changed how they operate, so check whether they are open before you visit.
